entities.name: Peter of Poitiers
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Peter of Poitiers (c. 1125/1130 – 1206) stands as a pivotal figure in the development of high scholasticism, succeeding the influential Peter Lombard as the "Master of the Sentences" at the nascent University of Paris. Born in Poitiers, France, his academic career unfolded during a period of profound intellectual ferment, as the cathedral schools of Paris were coalescing into Europe's first major universities. His significance lies in his role as a leading theologian and commentator, whose own *Sententiae* built upon and refined the systematic theological framework established by his predecessor, contributing to the standardization of Christian doctrine in the late 12th and early 13th centuries.

After initial studies, likely in his hometown, Peter of Poitiers gravitated to Paris, the undisputed intellectual capital of Latin Christendom, where he became a master of theology. By 1169, he was already noted as a prominent teacher, and by 1193, he had ascended to the prestigious position of Chancellor of Notre Dame, a role that granted him significant authority over academic appointments and the conferral of degrees. His principal work, known simply as *Sententiae*, comprised five books and served as a comprehensive theological textbook. It meticulously addressed key doctrines such as the Trinity, the Incarnation, creation, sin, and the sacraments, often engaging directly with Lombard's work while introducing his own unique perspectives and clarifications, particularly on the nature of God's essence and attributes.
